source.title: Instilling Inductive Biases with Subnetworks
source.authors: En-Yan Zhang; Michael A. Lepori; Ellie Pavlick

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper cites the grokking work and uses a related modular-arithmetic setting, but it does not measure delayed generalization, the formation of a generalizing circuit over training, or any other version of the claim.
record.gate_note: The arithmetic experiments report test accuracy under subnetwork transfer and related controls, but do not report the training-accuracy/test-accuracy timeline or delay that defines the claim. Their algorithmic-task accuracy and sample-efficiency results are recorded under fits_no_version. The vision results concern induced shape bias and do not test delayed generalization.
record.test_reason: The paper uses a Power et al.-style modular-arithmetic setup only as a testbed for subnetwork transfer (Subtask Induction). It reports final test accuracy against the number of disambiguation samples, with the best checkpoint kept from 100 epochs. It reports no train-versus-test timeline, no delayed generalization, no circuit-formation dynamics, and no weight-decay, initialization-scale or optimizer manipulation bearing on grokking. The vision experiments concern induced shape bias. No version of the claim is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that Subtask Induction instils inductive biases: better sample efficiency on modular arithmetic and a human-like shape bias in ResNet18 and ViT. It also beats data augmentation. They draw no conclusion about grokking.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses continuous-sparsification subnetwork discovery and transfers frozen subnetwork weights into a reinitialized model; it does not reproduce the grokking training setup or measure grokking.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different outcomes for different transferred subtasks and notes weaker, less stable transfer for one subnetwork localized from a model trained on a different computation.

fits_no_version.finding: Transferring a frozen discovered ab (mod p) subnetwork (3-8% of parameters) lets GPT-2 models reach near-perfect test accuracy on a2+ab (mod p) with about 1000 disambiguation samples. From-scratch models average 50.6% on the same data. Random subnetworks need about 6x more data. The transfer is at least as good as full-model transfer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Transferring a subnetwork implementing a constituent arithmetic subtask instils an inductive bias that improves sample efficiency on related modular-arithmetic tasks.

record.code_released: The paper says code and configuration files are released at an associated GitHub repository; URL not stated in the text.
record.problems: The arithmetic findings do not measure training-time grokking or the timing of a test-accuracy rise. Some results are presented in figures, and the main text reports aggregate rather than per-configuration numerical outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: Vision results on shape bias and cue-conflict performance were left out because they do not report delayed generalization. Additional arithmetic transfer conditions in Figures 8–10 were also left out because they concern subtask-transfer efficacy, not a version of the grokking claim.

untested.parts: Whether test accuracy jumps long after training accuracy saturates, and whether the delay grows with smaller training sets. No training curves are reported for the arithmetic task.
Gradual circuit formation, later removal of memorizing components, and progress measures.
Delays on non-algorithmic data, and switching via initialization scale or weight norm. The vision training curves (Fig. 5) show no delayed generalization claim.
Delayed generalization in LLM pretraining or fine-tuning.
Weight-decay efficiency account, critical dataset size, and ungrokking.
Whether runs converge to the same algorithm. Subnetworks are found by masking, but runs are not compared for algorithm identity.
Whether optimizer or numerical artifacts cause the delay.

record.verdict_notes: The study cites Power et al. 2022 and Nanda et al. 2023 only for the task format and as related interpretability work. The p=7 modulus and 1000-token inputs differ from grokking setups. Appendix C.2 mentions an early plateau in subnetwork-discovery accuracy, which the authors attribute to mask annealing; this is not grokking.

versions.untested_parts: Whether test accuracy rises long after training accuracy saturates, and whether delay grows as the training set shrinks.
Whether a generalizing circuit forms gradually, memorizing components are removed later, or progress measures anticipate a jump.
Whether grokking-like delays occur on non-algorithmic data or can be switched by initialization scale or weight norm.
Whether delayed generalization occurs during realistic large-model pretraining or fine-tuning.
Whether low-norm bias explains grokking, predicts a critical dataset size, or causes ungrokking.
Whether runs on the same task converge to the same identifiable algorithm rather than algorithms that vary with architecture or hyperparameters.
Whether optimizer or numerical choices cause the delay or its disappearance.

rows.subject: GPT-2 configurations (2 to 12 layers; aggregate across configurations)
rows.size_stated: 2 to 12 layers; embedding size 128; 4 attention heads; intermediate representation size 512
rows.stage_stated: trained on T2 after subnetwork transfer
rows.operation_detail: Transferred the discovered ab (mod p) subnetwork from a model trained on T1, then trained on T2.
rows.baseline: Models trained from scratch averaged 50.6% test accuracy on the same data.
rows.value: Subtask Induction achieved near-perfect accuracy with as few as 1000 disambiguation training samples (0.1% of total possible combinations).
rows.note: Reported as applying across all tested model configurations. This is an induced-bias sample-efficiency result, not a measurement of delayed generalization.
rows.check: The row compares the study's own method with a from-scratch control on sample efficiency. The value is the final best-checkpoint accuracy, not a delay after training accuracy saturates, so it cannot show grokking.

rows.subject: GPT-2 configurations (2 to 12 layers; aggregate across configurations)
rows.stage_stated: trained on T2 after transfer of a randomly sampled subnetwork
rows.operation_detail: Transferred a random subnetwork matched in parameter count and layer allocation to the discovered subnetwork, then trained on T2.
rows.measure: Disambiguation samples required to reach perfect generalization accuracy
rows.value: A randomly sampled subnetwork requires on average around 6 times as much data in order to reach perfect generalization accuracy.
rows.note: The comparison concerns sample efficiency of subnetwork transfer, not grokking delay.
rows.check: This is a method-versus-control comparison (about 6x more data needed for a random subnetwork). It is not a grokking measure.

rows.subject: GPT-2 configurations (2 to 12 layers; aggregate across configurations)
rows.stage_stated: trained on T2 after transfer of the full model trained on T1
rows.operation_detail: Transferred the entire T1-trained model and trained it on T2.
rows.value: Across sample sizes and model configurations, transferring subnetworks of around 3% to 7% of parameters achieves at least as good generalization accuracy and sample efficiency as transferring the entire model.
rows.note: Qualitative aggregate comparison; does not measure delayed generalization.
rows.check: This is a method-versus-full-model-transfer comparison. It is qualitative and unrelated to delayed generalization.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
